front: Bonding triangle axes?
back: ΔEN (vertical) against average EN (horizontal). Ionic top, metallic bottom-left, covalent bottom-right.

front: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?
back: Different-sized atoms disrupt layers so they cannot slide.

front: Polymer?
back: Macromolecule of many repeating monomer units.

front: Addition polymerisation?
back: C=C monomers join as double bonds open; no by-product.

front: (HL) Condensation polymerisation?
back: Bifunctional monomers join releasing H₂O/HCl: polyesters (ester links), polyamides (amide links).

front: Locating a binary compound on the bonding triangle?
back: Calculate ΔEN = |χ₁ − χ₂| and average χ = (χ₁ + χ₂)/2 from data booklet values; plot to read the predominant bonding type.

front: Where do CsF, Cl₂ and Na sit on the bonding triangle?
back: CsF: top (ionic, large ΔEN). Cl₂: bottom right (covalent, ΔEN = 0, high average EN). Na: bottom left (metallic).

front: Why is bonding described as a continuum?
back: Most substances have mixed character; e.g. AlCl₃ is ionic–covalent and SiO₂ polar covalent, so properties depend on position, not a single label.

front: Alloy?
back: A mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals (e.g. carbon), with metallic bonding — e.g. steel (Fe + C), brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn).

front: Why is stainless steel used for cutlery?
back: Chromium (and nickel) added to iron forms a protective oxide layer, so it resists corrosion; also harder than pure iron.

front: Do alloys have a sharp melting point?
back: Usually not — they melt over a range; often lower than the pure parent metal (e.g. solder).

front: Drawing the repeating unit of an addition polymer?
back: Draw the monomer with C=C turned into C–C, substituents kept, and continuation bonds through square brackets: e.g. propene → –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ–.

front: Monomers of PVC, PTFE and poly(ethene)?
back: PVC: chloroethene CH₂=CHCl. PTFE: tetrafluoroethene CF₂=CF₂. Poly(ethene): ethene CH₂=CH₂.

front: Why are addition polymers an environmental problem?
back: Strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds make them unreactive and non-biodegradable; combustion releases CO₂ (and HCl for PVC).

front: How can polymer properties be modified?
back: Chain length, branching (less branching → denser, stronger: HDPE vs LDPE), cross-linking, and adding plasticisers.

front: (HL) Monomers that form a polyamide?
back: A dicarboxylic acid (or diacyl chloride) + a diamine; each link –CONH– forms with loss of H₂O (or HCl). E.g. nylon-6,6, Kevlar.

front: (HL) Monomers that form a polyester?
back: A dicarboxylic acid + a diol; each ester link –COO– forms with loss of H₂O. E.g. PET from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and ethane-1,2-diol.

front: (HL) Natural condensation polymers?
back: Proteins (2-amino acids joined by amide/peptide links), polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose (glucose joined, losing water), and DNA.

front: (HL) Why are condensation polymers more biodegradable than addition polymers?
back: Their polar ester/amide links can be hydrolysed (by water, acid, base or enzymes) back to monomers.

front: (HL) Addition vs condensation polymerisation?
back: Addition: C=C monomers, polymer is the only product, same empirical formula as monomer. Condensation: two functional groups per monomer, a small molecule (H₂O/HCl) is also lost.
